units.title: The Excretory System
units.intro:
Excretion removes *metabolic* waste (CO₂, urea, excess salts and water). Egestion is undigested food — different word.

Organs: lungs (CO₂), skin (sweat: salts, a little urea), liver (makes urea from amino acids — deamination), kidneys (filter blood, keep what you still need).

cards.title: 6.1 The Excretory Products
body: All cells carry out metabolic reactions.
If these substances accumulate in the fluid surrounding the cells, they would become toxic (poisonous) and upset the homeostasis of the organism.
Single-celled organisms can remove their waste products by simple diffusion, but large animals require a more elaborate excretory system.
The external environment of a living organism is constantly changing.
The internal environment of the cells (the amount of water, the concentration of glucose, the temperature, etc.) is kept almost constant all the time.

cards.why: The liver breaks down old red blood cells (recycling iron and producing bile pigments) and deaminates excess amino acids to form urea. It also secretes bile to aid in fat digestion.

cards.title: 6.2 The Excretory Organs
body: The excretory organs in mammals are the skin, lungs, kidneys and liver.
The skin is considered to be the largest organ because it covers the entire surface of the body.
Human skin is composed of two layers: the epidermis and dermis.
The dermis is an inner layer, which is thicker than the epidermis.
The subcutaneous layer contains glands, as well as receptors and other skin structures.

cards.title: The Excretory Organs
body: Kidney: cortex → medulla → pelvis. Nephron: glomerulus filters, tubule reabsorbs glucose/amino acids/most water and salts, collecting duct adjusts water (ADH appears in Grade 11 homeostasis). Urine: water, urea, excess salts — not glucose in a healthy person.

cards.title: Filter then reclaim
body: If glucose appears in urine, the reclaim step failed (or was overloaded) — classic diabetes clue, tied later to insulin.

cards.title: More detail — kidney numbers in words
body: Urea comes from surplus amino acids: liver strips the nitrogen (deamination) and makes urea, which is less toxic than ammonia. Kidneys take a fraction of plasma in the glomerulus (filter under pressure). Useful solutes are pumped back in the tubule. Water follows by osmosis; ADH later fine-tunes the last duct. Bladder stores; sphincter is learned control.
Dialysis mimics the filter when both kidneys fail. Sweat cools you (Grade 11 temperature) and happens to carry some urea — it is not the main urea door.

cards.problem: One of the following is **not** part of the excretory organ in mammals.  A) Liver  B) Kidney  C) Skin  D) Stomach  E) Lung

steps.text: **Step 1.** The **stomach** is part of the digestive system, not the excretory system.
**Step 2.** Excretory organs remove metabolic waste (Kidneys: urea; Lungs: $$ CO_2 $$; Skin: sweat; Liver: processes toxins).

The medulla is a red colour and divides into a number of funnelshaped, hollow structures, called pyramids.
The dermis is an inner layer, which is thicker than the epidermis.
A nephron is a long, twisted, looping tubule and is the basic functional unit of the mammalian kidney.
Excretion is the process of getting rid of the waste products of metabolism.

tips.text: All cells constantly carry out metabolic reactions. These metabolic reactions produce waste products.
The main metabolic wastes in most mammals are carbon dioxide, excess water and salt, urea and red pigments.
Carbon dioxide and excess water are produced during cellular respiration.
The amino acids not used as a source of energy are catabolized in the liver by a process called deamination.
The nitrogen-containing part of the excess amino acid is combined with carbon dioxide and converted into urea, ammonia and uric acid.
The urea dissolves in the blood plasma and is taken to the kidneys to be excreted.
The liver also has many other functions.
The excretory system is responsible for the maintenance of homeostasis by selectively adjusting the concentration of substances in blood and other body fluids.

If allowed to accumulate, metabolic wastes would eventually reach toxic concentrations and upset the homeostasis of the organism. These waste products must, therefore, be removed from the body regularly by the process of excretion.

The excretory organs in mammals are the skin, lungs, kidneys and liver. However, the kidneys are the main excretory organs because they excrete nitrogenous wastes, excess water and mineral salts, and other substances in the form of urine.

questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes excretion from egestion (defecation) in a mammal?

options.A: Excretion removes undigested food that has passed through the alimentary canal, while egestion removes urea made in the liver.
options.B: Excretion removes metabolic wastes produced by chemical reactions inside the body cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.
options.C: Excretion removes only sweat and bile pigments, while egestion removes carbon dioxide and urea.
options.D: Excretion and egestion both remove the chemical waste products formed by reactions inside the body cells.

why: **Recall the definition of excretion.** Excretion is the biological process by which metabolic waste products, produced by chemical reactions inside the cells of the body, are removed. Typical examples are carbon dioxide, excess water and urea, and the process helps to maintain homeostasis.

**Recall the definition of egestion.** Egestion (defecation) is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that has simply passed through the alimentary canal and leaves the body as faeces. Like the empty grocery boxes in the house-cleaning analogy, this material never became part of the cells' activities.

**Test each option against the two definitions.** A reverses the two processes, so it is wrong. C is wrong because excretion also removes carbon dioxide and urea, not only sweat and bile pigments, and because egestion removes faeces, not carbon dioxide and urea. D is wrong because the materials removed by egestion were never products of reactions inside the cells.

**Select the one correct statement.** Only B matches the definitions exactly: excretion removes metabolic wastes made inside the cells, while egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A student in Asmara claims that defecation is a form of excretion because both processes remove unwanted material from the body. Correct the student's statement using the biological definitions of excretion and egestion.
questions.answer: Defecation (egestion) is not excretion. Egestion is the removal of undigested, unabsorbed food material that passed through the alimentary canal and never entered the body cells, whereas excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes such as carbon dioxide, excess water and urea that were produced by chemical reactions inside the cells. Only the second process is excretion.
why: **State what excretion removes.** Excretion removes metabolic waste products (for example carbon dioxide, excess water and urea) that are formed by chemical reactions inside the cells, and it maintains homeostasis.
**State what egestion removes.** Egestion removes undigested, unabsorbed food from the alimentary canal as faeces; this material passed through the gut without taking part in cell metabolism.

**Correct the student.** Because faeces are not products of chemical reactions inside the cells, defecation cannot be called excretion. The two processes differ in the origin of the material removed, not merely in the route by which it leaves the body.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Which one of the following materials is removed from the body by excretion and NOT by egestion?
questions.answer: B. Urea carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys
why: **Identify the origin of each material.** Excretion deals with wastes made by chemical reactions inside the cells; egestion deals with material that travelled through the alimentary canal without entering the cells.

**Classify the options.** A, C and D are all unabsorbed materials that simply pass along the alimentary canal, so they are removed by egestion. Urea, however, is made in the liver by deamination and is a metabolic waste carried in the blood plasma.
**Conclude.** Urea is the only listed material that is a product of cell metabolism, so B is the correct answer.

questions.q: Complete each of the following statements with the correct term. (a) Sweat, which consists of water, mineral salts and a small amount of urea, is produced by sweat glands located in the ______ layer of the skin. (b) The outer waterproof skin layer, which contains dead, keratinized cells, is the ______. (c) Urine passes from the pelvis of each kidney down to the urinary bladder through a tube called the ______.
why: **Identify the layer that contains the sweat glands.** The unit states that the thick inner dermis contains the sweat glands, blood vessels, hair roots and sensory nerve endings, so sweat is excreted through sweat glands in the dermis.
**Identify the outer waterproof layer.** The outermost layer is the epidermis, which is waterproof and contains dead, keratinized cells.

**Identify the tube that carries urine to the bladder.** Urine formed by the kidney collects in the pelvis and travels down a pair of ureters, one from each kidney, to the urinary bladder for temporary storage. The single tube that leaves the bladder is the urethra.
**Give the completed statements.** (a) dermis; (b) epidermis; (c) ureter. Note that the ureter must not be confused with the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: Complete the following statements about a longitudinal section of a mammalian kidney. (a) The dark red outer region that contains the spherical filtering units called nephrons is the ______. (b) The middle region that contains funnel-shaped, hollow structures called pyramids is the ______. (c) The white inner chamber that stores urine temporarily before it passes into the ureter is the ______.
why: **Recall the three regions in order.** A longitudinal section of a kidney shows the cortex outside, the medulla in the middle and the pelvis inside.

**Match each region to its description.** The cortex is the dark red outer region containing the nephrons; the medulla contains the pyramids; the pelvis is the white inner chamber that temporarily stores urine.
**State the answers.** (a) cortex; (b) medulla; (c) pelvis.

questions.q: Complete the following statements about the nephron. (a) The ball of blood capillaries enclosed by a double-walled cup is the ______. (b) The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the ______. (c) The single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body is the ______.
why: **Recall the structure of the nephron.** The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney and consists of the glomerulus enclosed in the Bowman's capsule, plus the renal tubule.
**Recall the glomerulus.** The glomerulus is a ball of blood capillaries enclosed by a double-walled cup called the Bowman's capsule, where ultrafiltration occurs.
**Recall the exit tube.** The urethra is the single tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside during urination; the ureters, by contrast, bring urine to the bladder.
**State the answers.** (a) glomerulus; (b) nephron; (c) urethra.

questions.q: During a hot afternoon shift on the salt flats near Massawa, a labourer loses $$3.2\ \text{liters}$$ of sweat. In this sweat, mineral salts (NaCl) make up $$0.30\%$$ of the mass and urea makes up $$0.05\%$$ of the mass. Given that $$1\ \text{L} = 1000\ \text{mL}$$ and that $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost, (b) the mass of urea lost, and (c) the total mass of these two substances lost in the sweat.
questions.answer: (a) $$9.6\ \text{g}$$ of mineral salts; (b) $$1.6\ \text{g}$$ of urea; (c) $$11.2\ \text{g}$$ in total.
why: **Convert the volume of sweat into a mass.** The volume is $$3.2\ \text{L} = 3.2 \times 1000 = 3200\ \text{mL}$$. Since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the total mass of sweat is $$3200\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 3200\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of mineral salts.** Mineral salts are $$0.30\%$$ of the mass, so mass of salts $$= \frac{0.30}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0030 \times 3200 = 9.6\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of urea.** Urea is $$0.05\%$$ of the mass, so mass of urea $$= \frac{0.05}{100} \times 3200\ \text{g} = 0.0005 \times 3200 = 1.6\ \text{g}$$.
**Add the two masses.** Total mass lost $$= 9.6\ \text{g} + 1.6\ \text{g} = 11.2\ \text{g}$$.

**Interpret the result biologically.** The sweat glands in the dermis have removed water, mineral salts and a small amount of urea from the blood. This shows the skin acting both as an organ of excretion (removing metabolic waste) and as a means of cooling the body by evaporation.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A student in Asmara walks home quickly on a warm afternoon and loses $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of sweat. The sweat contains $$0.25\%$$ mineral salts and $$0.04\%$$ urea by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate (a) the mass of mineral salts lost and (b) the mass of urea lost.
why: **Convert the volume of sweat to mass.** $$0.8\ \text{L} = 800\ \text{mL}$$, and since $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of sweat has a mass of $$1\ \text{g}$$, the mass of sweat is $$800\ \text{g}$$.
**Find the mass of mineral salts.** Mass of salts $$= 0.25\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.25}{100} \times 800 = 2.0\ \text{g}$$.
**Find the mass of urea.** Mass of urea $$= 0.04\% \times 800\ \text{g} = \frac{0.04}{100} \times 800 = 0.32\ \text{g}$$.
**State the conclusion.** The smaller sweat loss removes $$2.0\ \text{g}$$ of salts and $$0.32\ \text{g}$$ of urea, still showing that sweat carries away mineral salts and a trace of metabolic waste.

questions.q: A healthy adult living in Keren excretes $$1.5\ \text{L}$$ of urine in one day. The urine contains $$2.0\%$$ urea and $$0.9\%$$ mineral salts by mass. Taking $$1\ \text{mL}$$ of urine as $$1\ \text{g}$$, calculate the total mass of dissolved waste (urea plus mineral salts) excreted in the urine that day.
questions.answer: $$43.5\ \text{g}$$ in total ($$30\ \text{g}$$ urea and $$13.5\ \text{g}$$ mineral salts).
why: **Convert the urine volume into a mass.** $$1.5\ \text{L} = 1500\ \text{mL}$$, so the mass of urine is $$1500\ \text{mL} \times 1\ \text{g/mL} = 1500\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of urea.** Mass of urea $$= \frac{2.0}{100} \times 1500 = 30\ \text{g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of mineral salts.** Mass of salts $$= \frac{0.9}{100} \times 1500 = 13.5\ \text{g}$$.
**Add the two masses.** Total dissolved waste $$= 30\ \text{g} + 13.5\ \text{g} = 43.5\ \text{g}$$, all of it carried in the urine formed by the kidneys.

questions.q: A camel kept near the hot coastal town of Massawa can go for many days with very little drinking water, while a dairy cow kept in the cool highlands of Asmara must drink frequently. Using the structure of the nephron and the process of osmoregulation, explain how the camel's extensive, extremely long loop of Henle allows it to survive on so little water.
questions.answer: The camel's very long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla and maintains a steep concentration gradient there, so a large amount of water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood. The camel therefore produces a small volume of highly concentrated urine and loses very little water. The cow's shorter loop of Henle produces only a small gradient, so less water is reabsorbed, more dilute urine is formed, and the cow must drink frequently.
why: **Recall where water is reabsorbed in the nephron.** The unit states that in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, and that the loop of Henle is the region responsible for osmoregulation (water balance).

**Relate loop length to the concentration gradient.** The camel's extremely long loop of Henle extends deep into the medulla of the kidney. Because the loop is so long, it builds and maintains a very steep concentration gradient in the medulla.

**Explain the osmotic movement of water.** The steep gradient draws water out of the collecting duct and back into the surrounding blood capillaries by osmosis, so a very large proportion of the water in the filtrate is returned to the blood instead of being lost.

**Link this to the volume and concentration of urine.** Because so much water is reabsorbed, the camel produces only a small volume of highly concentrated urine. Its water loss is therefore minimised, which is the advantage needed in a dry desert environment.

**Contrast with the cow.** The cow has a much shorter loop of Henle, so only a small concentration gradient is maintained in the medulla. Less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, more dilute urine is produced in a larger volume, and the cow must therefore drink frequently to replace the water it loses.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon in Massawa a worker sweats heavily and produces only a small volume of concentrated urine, but on a cool morning in Asmara the same worker produces a larger volume of dilute urine. Explain this difference in terms of osmoregulation in the nephron.
questions.answer: Heavy sweating removes a large volume of water from the blood, so the blood becomes more concentrated. In the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, more water is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis, leaving a small volume of highly concentrated urine. On the cool morning little water is lost by sweating, less water is reabsorbed by osmosis, and a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. In this way the nephron keeps the water content of the body constant.
why: **State the effect of heavy sweating.** Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating on a hot day removes a large amount of water from the blood and body fluids.
**Locate the site of water reabsorption.** Water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct, with the loop of Henle responsible for osmoregulation.

**Explain the hot-day response.** Because the blood has lost water, more water is drawn back from the filtrate by osmosis, so a small volume of highly concentrated urine is formed and water is conserved.

**Explain the cool-day response and conclude.** With little water lost by sweating, less reabsorption by osmosis is needed, so a larger volume of dilute urine is produced. The nephron therefore maintains a constant internal water balance (homeostasis).

questions.q: Describe the two main processes that take place in a nephron, ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption, stating clearly where each occurs and what each achieves.
questions.answer: Ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule: the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, creating high blood pressure that forces water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea out of the capillaries into the Bowman's capsule to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins remain in the blood. Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule: all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are actively transported back into the surrounding blood capillaries, so useful materials are not lost from the body.
why: **Define ultrafiltration and give its site.** Ultrafiltration is high-pressure physical filtering that occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.

**Explain how the pressure is produced.** The afferent arteriole entering the glomerulus is wider than the efferent arteriole leaving it, which creates high blood pressure inside the glomerular capillaries.

**State what passes through and what is held back.** Water, glucose, amino acids, mineral salts and urea are forced out to form the glomerular filtrate, while red blood cells and large proteins are too large to pass through the pores and stay in the blood.

**Define selective reabsorption and give its site.** Selective reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, where all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are taken back into the blood capillaries by active transport.

**State what is achieved.** Together the two processes remove nitrogenous waste and excess water and salts from the blood while returning useful materials such as glucose and amino acids to the body, which is why glucose is absent from the urine of a healthy person.

questions.q: Both kidneys of a healthy adult living in Asmara produce about $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate every day. During one particular day this adult excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.35\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from the body on that day. (b) Express this total fluid loss as a percentage of the daily volume of glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain, using the events in the nephron, why the volume of fluid actually lost is so much smaller than the volume of filtrate produced.
questions.answer: (a) $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$1.58\%$$ of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Over $$99\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood because glucose, amino acids and essential mineral salts are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct; only a small volume is finally excreted as urine, sweat and water vapour.
why: **List the measured fluid losses.** Urine $$= 1.6\ \text{L}$$, sweat $$= 0.9\ \text{L}$$ and water vapour in expired air $$= 0.35\ \text{L}$$. All three are measured in the same unit, so they can be added directly.
**Calculate the total volume lost (part a).** Total volume lost $$= 1.6\ \text{L} + 0.9\ \text{L} + 0.35\ \text{L} = 2.85\ \text{L}$$.
**Set up the percentage calculation (part b).** Percentage lost $$= \frac{\text{total volume lost}}{\text{volume of glomerular filtrate}} \times 100 = \frac{2.85}{180} \times 100$$.

**Complete the arithmetic.** $$\frac{2.85}{180} = 0.01583$$, and $$0.01583 \times 100 = 1.583\%$$, which rounds to approximately $$1.58\%$$. This means well over $$98\%$$ of the filtrate never leaves the body.

**Explain the fate of the filtrate in the nephron (part c).** As the filtrate flows through the proximal convoluted tubule, all glucose, all amino acids and essential mineral salts are returned to the surrounding blood capillaries by active transport (selective reabsorption). In the loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, water is reabsorbed by osmosis. More than $$99\%$$ of the filtered water is therefore returned to the blood.

**Link the explanation to the numbers.** Of the $$180\ \text{L}$$ filtered, only $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ leaves as urine, so about $$178.4\ \text{L}$$ is reabsorbed. The remaining losses as sweat and water vapour are small additional losses from the body fluids. This high efficiency of reabsorption is what allows the body to lose only about $$2.85\ \text{L}$$ from a filtrate volume of $$180\ \text{L}$$.

questions.q: Both kidneys of a labourer working in Massawa produce $$180\ \text{liters}$$ of glomerular filtrate in one day. On that day he excretes $$0.9\ \text{L}$$ of urine, loses $$2.4\ \text{L}$$ of sweat and about $$0.45\ \text{L}$$ of water vapour in expired air. (a) Calculate the total volume of fluid lost from his body. (b) Express this total as a percentage of the daily glomerular filtrate. (c) Explain why sweating heavily on a hot day leads to the production of a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
questions.answer: (a) $$3.75\ \text{L}$$ of fluid is lost in total. (b) This is approximately $$2.08\%$$ of the glomerular filtrate. (c) Heavy sweating removes water from the blood; in response, more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct back into the blood, so a smaller volume of more concentrated urine is produced and water is conserved.
why: **Add the three fluid losses.** Total volume lost $$= 0.9\ \text{L} + 2.4\ \text{L} + 0.45\ \text{L} = 3.75\ \text{L}$$.
**Set up the percentage.** Percentage lost $$= \frac{3.75}{180} \times 100$$.

**Complete the arithmetic.** $$\frac{3.75}{180} = 0.02083$$, so the percentage is $$2.083\%$$, approximately $$2.08\%$$. Even with heavy sweating, more than $$97\%$$ of the filtrate is returned to the blood.

**Explain the effect of sweating on urine.** Sweat consists mainly of water, so heavy sweating lowers the water content of the blood. More water is then reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, leaving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

**Conclude on osmoregulation.** The kidney adjusts the volume of water reabsorbed so that the water content of the body stays constant; this is osmoregulation, and it protects the body from dehydration on a hot day.

questions.q: A nurse in Asmara records the fluid output of a patient over two days. On the cool day the patient forms $$180\ \text{L}$$ of glomerular filtrate and excretes $$1.6\ \text{L}$$ of urine; on the hot day the same volume of filtrate is formed, but only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of urine is excreted. (a) Calculate the volume of filtrate returned to the blood on each day. (b) Explain, using the nephron, why less urine is formed on the hot day.
questions.answer: (a) Cool day: $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. Hot day: $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$ reabsorbed. (b) On the hot day more water is lost from the body, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis from the collecting duct back into the blood, leaving less water in the filtrate and therefore a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.
why: **State the relationship between filtrate, urine and reabsorption.** Volume reabsorbed $$=$$ volume of glomerular filtrate $$-$$ volume of urine excreted.
**Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the cool day.** $$180\ \text{L} - 1.6\ \text{L} = 178.4\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{178.4}{180} \times 100 = 99.1\%$$ of the filtrate.
**Calculate the reabsorbed volume for the hot day.** $$180\ \text{L} - 0.8\ \text{L} = 179.2\ \text{L}$$, which is $$\frac{179.2}{180} \times 100 = 99.6\%$$ of the filtrate.

**Explain the difference using the nephron.** The loop of Henle maintains a concentration gradient in the medulla, and water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. On the hot day the body has lost more water, so a greater proportion is reabsorbed and only $$0.8\ \text{L}$$ of concentrated urine remains to be excreted.
